NGC457.answer: φ Cassiopeiae is probably just that, since Gaia's measurement puts it at the cluster's distance, out in the Perseus arm. That would make it one of the most luminous stars in the galaxy, bright enough to reach your naked eye across the gap between two arms. The case is not quite closed, which only makes that pinpoint more intriguing.
NGC457.story: Distance is not the only toll on this light, for the dust along this line of sight soaks up roughly three quarters of it on the way. A star still bright enough for the naked eye after crossing that much distance and that much dust would have to shine well over a hundred thousand times as brightly as the Sun.

NGC4755.beat: The next arm in, beside the dark
NGC4755.question: How can the Jewel Box sparkle right at the edge of the Coalsack's shadow?
NGC4755.why: The Jewel Box sits just outside the Coalsack's edge, and the two together show two depths of the disk in one field.
NGC4755.look: Start at Mimosa on the eastern arm of the Cross and nudge just over a degree south-east to a compact letter A of stars, one of them orange. Sweep a little south and the star fields fade into the Coalsack's darkness.
NGC4755.answer: The two are nowhere near each other: the Coalsack is a dust cloud about 500 light-years away, while the Jewel Box lies more than twelve times farther, in the next arm in. From here the young cluster just peeks out past the cloud's edge, one of the many lamps of the inner arm that the dust lets through.
NGC4755.story: Its distance comes from Gaia's parallaxes, averaged over hundreds of members, and from matching its hot stars against nearer young families. Both put it on the arm that runs inward of ours through Centaurus and Carina. Clusters as young as this one are the most trusted markers of an arm, because they have not had time to drift away from it.

NGC5128.beat: Beyond: a different kind of galaxy
NGC5128.question: Is every galaxy a flat spiral like the Milky Way?
NGC5128.why: Centaurus A is a faint oval glow a few degrees north of Omega Centauri, and it is built quite differently from our own galaxy.
NGC5128.look: Start at Omega Centauri and move about four and a half degrees north. Under a dark sky binoculars show a small, slightly oval glow that swells with averted vision.
NGC5128.answer: Centaurus A is a giant elliptical, a vast rounded swarm of stars rather than a thin spinning disk, and the nearest galaxy of its kind. Spirals like ours, with their arms and nurseries, are only one of the ways a galaxy can be built.
NGC5128.story: Giant ellipticals are thought to grow by mergers, and Centaurus A shows the evidence: a lane of dust and young stars cuts across its middle, the remains of a gas-rich spiral it swallowed. Our own galaxy has eaten only small neighbors so far, but its merger with Andromeda, billions of years from now, may leave something rather like this.

NGC5139.beat: The halo: a lost galaxy's heart
NGC5139.question: Could the grandest globular in our sky be what is left of another galaxy?
NGC5139.why: Omega Centauri is the biggest and brightest globular cluster of the Milky Way, and its stars do not follow the rules that ordinary globulars keep.
NGC5139.look: To the eye it is a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow brightening steadily toward the center, like a snowball, grainy at the edge under a dark sky.
NGC5139.answer: Omega Centauri, about 17,700 light-years from us, may well be just that. Its several generations of stars and its backward orbit around the galaxy fit the core of a small galaxy that merged with the young Milky Way and was stripped of everything but its dense heart. If so, the halo holds the remains of the galaxies ours has eaten, and Omega Centauri is the largest of them you can see by eye.
NGC5139.story: In 2019 astronomers sifting Gaia's measurements found a faint river of stars, named Fimbulthul, stretching across tens of degrees of the southern sky. Its stars share Omega Centauri's motion and, as later spectra showed, its unusual mix of chemistry. It is a tail pulled off the cluster by the Milky Way's tides, still tracing the orbit the cluster has followed for billions of years.

NGC6231.beat: The next arm in, behind our own
NGC6231.question: Which of the bright stars around NGC 6231 belong to the next spiral arm?
NGC6231.why: NGC 6231 is a compact knot of brilliant young stars at the tail of Scorpius, and the bright stars around it come from two very different depths.
NGC6231.look: Follow Scorpius's tail to the naked-eye pair ζ¹ and ζ² Scorpii, then go half a degree north to a compact knot of a dozen bright stars over fainter ones. Compare the two ζ stars: one orange, one pale.
NGC6231.answer: NGC 6231 and the paler ζ¹ do, both about 5,190 light-years away at the core of a group of hot young stars in the next arm in, while orange ζ² is a nearby giant in our own stretch of the disk. ζ¹ looks pale rather than blue because dust along that long road reddens its light, and a single glance here spans the gap between two spiral arms.
NGC6231.story: This cluster is the core of a sprawling association of hot young stars spread over a few hundred light-years along the next arm in. Associations like it are so young that they still sit where their birth clouds were, which makes them the brightest markers astronomers have for plotting where an arm runs.

NGC6397.beat: The halo, dated by its embers
NGC6397.question: How old is the galaxy's halo, judged by its dying embers?
NGC6397.why: NGC 6397 is one of the nearest globular clusters, a bright, ragged glow in Ara, close enough for Hubble to see its dimmest dead stars.
NGC6397.look: From β Arae, below Scorpius' tail, sweep about three degrees north-east to a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo. From mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon, while from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
NGC6397.answer: The embers say about 11.5 billion years: the faintest white dwarfs Hubble found in NGC 6397 have been cooling that long, and fits to its living stars give an even older figure. The halo's clusters formed in the galaxy's first few billion years, and the disk is the younger structure that grew inside them.
NGC6397.story: NGC 6397 also carries a clock of a stranger kind, the rare element beryllium, made when cosmic rays from the galaxy's first exploding stars shattered atoms of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Its amount built up steadily as time passed, and in 2004 astronomers used the beryllium in this cluster's stars to estimate that it formed only a few hundred million years after the galaxy's first stars.

NGC7000.question: What does a working stretch of our own spiral arm look like?
NGC7000.why: The North America Nebula is one of the nurseries of the Cygnus Milky Way, and it shows what our own arm is doing in our era rather than long ago.
NGC7000.look: Put Deneb at the edge of a wide field and look about 3° east. On a dark, transparent night the area looks slightly brighter than the surrounding Milky Way, with a sharper dark edge on its southern side. A nebula filter helps, and rich star fields should not be mistaken for the glow.
NGC7000.answer: A working stretch of arm looks much like this faint glow: a cloud of hydrogen about 2,640 light-years away, lit by hot young stars that have switched on inside it and still wrapped in lanes of dust. Glowing gas, fresh stars and dark dust together are the signature of a spiral arm, and from inside one, that mixture is what the band of Cygnus is made of.
NGC7000.story: Nurseries glow red in photographs because hydrogen gives off a deep red light when electrons fall back into atoms that ultraviolet starlight had torn apart. That color is how astronomers find nurseries across a galaxy. In face-on spirals the red knots line up along the arms like beads; in ours they crowd the band of Cygnus because we look along the arm.

NGC752.question: Why does an old cluster like NGC 752 sit so far from the Milky Way's band?
NGC752.why: NGC 752 is far older than the clusters strung along the band, and its position is a record of what time does to a star family's orbit.
NGC752.look: Start at the wide orange pair 56 Andromedae in southern Andromeda and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. Then notice where you are: the band of the Milky Way runs well to the north, through Cassiopeia and Perseus.
NGC752.answer: Time has pushed it there, because every passage near a massive cloud or through a spiral arm gives a cluster a small kick. Over more than a billion years those kicks have let NGC 752, about 1,414 light-years away, bob far above and below the thin layer where it was born. Young clusters hug the band and old ones wander, so a cluster's height above the plane is a rough clock of its age.
NGC752.story: Astronomers call this disk heating, and they measure it by comparing families and single stars of different ages. The spread of their up-and-down speeds grows steadily with age, so the oldest members of the disk bob highest above its midplane. This cluster's place far from the band, and the motion Gaia measures for it, fit that pattern.

NGC869.question: What lies across the quiet gap beyond our own spiral arm?
NGC869.why: The Double Cluster is one of the finest binocular sights of the northern sky, and it lies much farther away than its brightness suggests.
NGC869.look: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, a few of them orange. Lower the binoculars and the naked eye still shows them as a hazy patch in the Milky Way.
NGC869.answer: The Perseus arm does, and the Double Cluster is its brightest landmark in our sky: these clusters belong to the next arm out from the center, across a gap where far fewer young stars shine. Past Perseus the disk thins toward its outer edge, so in this direction the rich clusters give out sooner than they do toward Sagittarius.
NGC869.story: The distance to the arm beyond the gap was one of the early triumphs of radio parallaxes. In 2006 a maser in a nursery in this part of the sky gave a distance by pure geometry, and it settled a long argument by showing that arm to be nearer than older estimates based on the speed of its gas. Gaia's distance to the Double Cluster now fits the same lane.

NGC884.beat: The next arm out: one burst
NGC884.question: How big a stretch of spiral arm can light up in one burst of star birth?
NGC884.why: χ Persei is the eastern twin of the Double Cluster, and its twin is only the start of its family.
NGC884.look: Keep both clusters in the field and compare: χ Persei is a little looser than h. Then sweep slowly around the pair at low power, where a sprinkling of bright stars spreads across the surrounding field.
NGC884.answer: A whole region of the arm can switch on together: both clusters and a wide halo of stars around them share one age, so a large patch of the Perseus arm formed its stars in a single burst. Bursts like this are how spiral arms light up, and seen from outside they would be the bright knots that mark an arm in a photograph of a galaxy.
NGC884.story: A burst that big needs a big cloud. A giant cloud usually turns only a few percent of its gas into stars, so two rich clusters and the scattered family around them point to a parent of hundreds of thousands of Suns' worth of gas. Clouds that heavy gather mostly where a spiral arm sweeps gas together.

SMC.beat: Beyond: the galaxy that measured ours
SMC.question: How did this little galaxy help map our own?
SMC.why: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a companion galaxy of the Milky Way, and in the story of finding our place it plays a surprising part.
SMC.look: Under a dark sky it looks like a small torn-off cloud; binoculars show a soft, uneven glow, brighter along one side, with 47 Tucanae and NGC 362, two globulars of our own halo, as fuzzy stars beside it.
SMC.answer: Leavitt's rule gave astronomers lamps of known power, and Harlow Shapley used that kind of yardstick to measure the distances of globular clusters and place the center of the galaxy far off in Sagittarius. The Cloud itself is one of the small companion galaxies that circle our own, near enough that its brightest stars could be timed one by one.
SMC.story: Leavitt's rule said only which Cepheids were truly brighter than others, not how bright any of them actually was, so the scale still floated free. In 1913 Ejnar Hertzsprung pinned it down from the slow drift of a dozen or so nearby Cepheids across the sky, and with that one fixed point the rule became a working yardstick.

STAR-Arcturus.question: Is every star near the Sun a local, or are some just passing through?
STAR-Arcturus.why: Arcturus is a near neighbor and one of the brightest stars of the sky, yet it does not move like the stars around it, and that difference opens a window on the galaxy's layers.
STAR-Arcturus.look: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes, and hold it in the field: its orange-gold is obvious. It sits far from the Milky Way's band, in a part of the sky that looks up and out of the disk rather than along it.
STAR-Arcturus.answer: Some are just passing through, and Arcturus is the brightest of them. It only happens to be crossing our neighborhood now, on an orbit that climbs higher above and below the disk's thin middle layer than the Sun ever goes. The galaxy is layered, a young thin disk inside an older, thicker one and an ancient halo around both, and the Sun belongs to the thin, young layer.
STAR-Arcturus.story: Arcturus does not travel alone, for dozens of other old stars share its unusual motion, a group astronomers call the Arcturus stream. They still debate whether it is debris from a small galaxy swallowed long ago or stars stirred into step by the bar at the galaxy's center. Either way, the Sun's neighborhood turns out to be a crossroads where stars of very different origins pass through.

STAR-Fomalhaut.beat: Home: looking out of the disk
STAR-Fomalhaut.question: Why does Fomalhaut stand so alone in its part of the sky?
STAR-Fomalhaut.why: Fomalhaut is a close neighbor of the Sun, but what makes it useful here is the empty sky around it.
STAR-Fomalhaut.look: Follow the west side of the Great Square of Pegasus about 45° south to Fomalhaut, the only bright star in that stretch. Sweep the binoculars around it and compare the sparse field with any patch of the Milky Way: far fewer faint stars fill the view.
STAR-Fomalhaut.answer: That part of the sky points well away from the plane of the disk, so after a few neighbors like Fomalhaut, about 25 light-years away, the line of sight runs out of stars quickly. Where the disk thins out the universe beyond opens up, and faint galaxies such as the Sculptor Galaxy hide not far to the east.
STAR-Fomalhaut.story: You can test this with nothing but a count: a binocular field near Fomalhaut holds only a fraction of the faint stars that crowd an equal field in Cygnus or Sagittarius. William Herschel made the same count with a telescope in the 1780s, sampling the sky field by field, and concluded that we live inside a flattened system of stars, the first rough map of the Milky Way.

STAR-Procyon.beat: Home: a neighbor at the band's edge
STAR-Procyon.question: Procyon sits at the edge of the winter Milky Way, so is it part of it?
STAR-Procyon.why: Procyon is one of the closest bright stars to the Sun, and it shines right beside the faint river of the winter Milky Way in Canis Minor and Monoceros.
STAR-Procyon.look: Find Procyon, the eastern corner of the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse. On a dark night the faint band of the winter Milky Way runs just to its west through Monoceros, a soft glow beside a brilliant point.
STAR-Procyon.answer: It belongs to the galaxy, as every star you see does, but not to that glow: Procyon is a close neighbor, while the band beside it is made of stars hundreds of times farther along the disk. Near stars lie all over our sky because we sit inside the disk's thickness, and only the distant ones pile up into a band.
STAR-Procyon.story: From Procyon our Sun would be a modest star, a little fainter than Polaris looks to us, in what we call Aquila, on the opposite side of the sky, and the Milky Way would look almost exactly as it does to us. A few light-years barely change the view of the galaxy, which is the clearest sign that the band is very far away and the neighbors are very close.

STAR-Sirius.question: Why are the Sun's nearest neighbors scattered all over the sky instead of along the band?
STAR-Sirius.why: Sirius outshines every other star of the night, yet it is not a giant beacon but a neighbor, and neighbors are the first clue to the shape of the thing we live in.
STAR-Sirius.look: Follow Orion's Belt down and to the left to Sirius, and park it near the edge of the field to tame the glare. Then lower the binoculars and notice where the brightest winter stars lie: Sirius, Procyon, Capella and Aldebaran are spread widely, some well away from the faint winter band of the Milky Way.
STAR-Sirius.answer: They are too close to show it: Sirius and the other near stars lie well within the thickness of the disk, so from where we sit they surround us in every direction, like the trees right around you in a forest. Only stars thousands of light-years off crowd into a band, and that crowding is the next clue to the shape of our galaxy.
STAR-Sirius.story: Astronomers have counted the Sun's neighbors with care, and out to about twenty light-years there are roughly a hundred known stars, most of them faint red dwarfs no eye can see. Infrared surveys still turn up new ones, cool brown dwarfs only a few light-years away. The neighbors we can see by eye are the rare bright exceptions, Sirius chief among them.

Stock2.beat: Our arm, next to the next arm
Stock2.question: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster share a sweep, but do they share an arm?
Stock2.why: Stock 2 is a big, loose family just north of the Double Cluster, and the pair is the clearest demonstration in the northern sky of how deep the band runs.
Stock2.look: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north until a large, loose group fills much of the view, the stick figure some call the Muscleman. Sweep back and forth between them: Stock 2's stars look bright and coarse, the Double Cluster's small and densely packed.
Stock2.answer: Stock 2 belongs to our own arm, while the Double Cluster lies across the gap in the Perseus arm, the next one out from the center. The difference in sparkle you just saw is the gap between two spiral arms, squeezed by perspective into two degrees of sky.
Stock2.story: Plot the young clusters in this part of the sky by their Gaia distances and they fall into two groups, one nearer than about three thousand light-years and one from about six to nine thousand, with few in between. Young families mark where arms are because they have had no time to wander away, so a stretch of distance with almost none of them is a landmark in its own right.
